Know more about the
"Prinsesa ng Baybay"
landmark.title: Ang Prinsesa ng Baybay
landmark.subtitle: The story behind the statue on the Puerto Princesa Baywalk.
landmark.historyHeading: How the statue came to be
history: Ang Prinsesa ng Baybay ("The Princess of the Shore") is the fiberglass statue of a woman with windswept hair, playing with birds, that stands at the far end of the Puerto Princesa Baywalk — the City Coastal Reclamation Area, the city’s own version of Manila’s Roxas Boulevard.

The statue draws on local folklore about how the city got its name: seafarers were said to see a princess-like maiden walking along the bay late in the afternoon or early evening, who would seem to vanish whenever anyone approached. The Rotary Club of Puerto Princesa commissioned the statue in 2007 as a symbol of that story and of Palaweño life and culture more broadly, unveiling it on December 7, 2007.
trivia: The Rotary Club of Puerto Princesa initiated the project in 2007, under then-president Bobby Castro, hoping to give the city a landmark on the scale of Singapore’s Merlion or Denmark’s Little Mermaid.
The design was chosen through a public contest launched on July 13, 2007, under the theme "Simbolo ng Ating Kultura at Buhay" (Symbol of Our Culture and Life).
The winning concept combined designs from two artists: Zaldy Jumawan, then based in Palawan, and Elordie Mesac, a Tagbanua artist trained under Charles Wandag’s Aborlan Arts Program.
The statue’s face was deliberately sculpted with the flat nose characteristic of the Tagbanua people, Puerto Princesa’s original inhabitants.
The final 100-kilogram fiberglass statue was executed by Manila-based sculptor Ronel F. Roces and unveiled on December 7, 2007, at the City Coastal Reclamation Area — the Baywalk.
Both original designers reportedly felt the finished sculpture strayed from their concept of a princess watching the sunset with birds in the background.

miningWatch.title: Mining Watch
miningWatch.subtitle: Tracking how mining is affecting Palawan's environment, communities, and Indigenous peoples.
miningWatch.disclaimer: This page is compiled from independent journalism and human-rights/environmental organizations for public awareness. It is not an official statement or position of the City Government of Puerto Princesa.
miningWatch.mapCaveat: Each pin marks a known mining site at the barangay or town level, based on MGB records and the news reports listed below. Locations are approximate, not exact concession boundaries. Tap a pin for details and sources.
miningWatch.forestLossSubtitle: Tree cover lost across Palawan from 2001 to 2025, grouped by main cause. Some causes remove forest for good, like farms, mines and settlements. Others, like logging and fire, leave land that can grow back.
miningWatch.forestLossMiningNote: Mining and energy projects (shown as "Hard commodities") cleared the least forest of any cause: about 1,257 of the roughly 224,000 hectares lost since 2001. Farming and shifting cultivation cleared far more. That figure likely understates what mining does. The 11 companies now operating in Palawan hold about 29,430 hectares in concessions, and most of it is not cleared yet. Mining roads also open remote forest to logging and farming, and this chart counts that clearing under those causes instead. Mining also targets old-growth forest and protected ancestral land, including Mt. Mantalingahan, Bataraza and Brooke's Point (see the map above). Its damage spreads past the cleared area through polluted water, like the hexavalent chromium found near Rio Tuba (see the articles below).
miningWatch.footerNote: Every article below links to its original, independently published source. If you spot an outdated or broken link, please open an issue on this project's GitHub repository.
context: Palawan is often called the Philippines' last ecological frontier. It is a UNESCO Man and Biosphere Reserve with nearly half of the country's remaining old-growth forest, 30 percent of its mangroves, and 40 percent of its coral reefs. It also sits on some of the world's largest untapped nickel deposits, and demand for nickel keeps rising because of electric-vehicle batteries. That is why large-scale mining has been one of the most disputed issues in the province for decades.

Puerto Princesa has its own warning story. The city was home to the Palawan Quicksilver Mines Inc. mercury mine, closed since 1976, and residents living near it were later found to have mercury poisoning. In March 2025, after decades of campaigning, the provincial government signed a 50-year moratorium on new mining agreements and exploration permits. The ban has limits. It does not cover Puerto Princesa, which as a highly urbanized city is outside provincial control. It does not affect the 11 mines already operating elsewhere in Palawan. And the Palawan Council for Sustainable Development can still grant clearances, which critics say could let new projects through.

The articles below, from independent journalists and from human-rights and environmental groups, follow how that fight is going: in the courts, on Indigenous ancestral land, and in the rivers and reefs downstream of the mines.
